turns.content: For three interacting nucleons at unspecified energy and partial wave, can two-body binding by itself determine whether a three-body bound state exists? What two logical directions must be tested?
What general theoretical strategy can resolve those two implication directions when the interaction details are unspecified?
Define propositions B2 and B3 for two-body-subsystem binding and three-body binding, and write the necessity and sufficiency implications explicitly.
Can a three-nucleon bound state exist even when none of its two-nucleon subsystems is bound? What does that imply about the necessity of two-body binding?
In the reverse direction, does a bound two-nucleon subsystem alone guarantee a bound three-nucleon state? What does that imply about sufficiency?
Why do interactions among the three nucleons, together with the unspecified energy and partial wave, keep both implication tests relevant?
Combine the two implication checks into the most defensible general conclusion about three-body binding when two-body subsystems are bound or unbound.
Name a recognized few-body phenomenon showing that pairwise binding is not necessary, and explain why unspecified dynamics prevent pairwise binding from being sufficient.
State the final logical relationship between two-body and three-body binding under the information supplied.
